concepts.title: Prompt Engineering Principles: Specificity, Examples, and Structure
concepts.description: Prompt engineering is applied conditioning: specificity, well-chosen few-shot examples, and clear output structure all work by narrowing the space of plausible next-token continuations toward the behavior you want, not by being more polite or more verbose.
learningObjectives: Explain, in terms of the next-token-prediction mechanism, why vague prompts produce inconsistent output across repeated calls.
Apply specificity techniques -- explicit role, constraints, format, and things to avoid -- to reliably tighten a prompt's behavior.
Design effective few-shot examples and explain both why they work and the biased-example pitfall that undermines them.
Request structured output (e.g. JSON matching a schema) reliably, and defensively handle the cases where it still isn't valid.
Diagnose a poorly-performing prompt and identify which principle -- specificity, examples, or structure -- is being violated.

sections.heading: Specificity: Why Vague Prompts Produce Inconsistent Output
sections.body:
Every word in a prompt conditions the probability distribution over what comes next (the mechanism from the previous module), and prompt engineering is the practical craft of using that on purpose. A vague prompt like 'write about dogs' leaves most of the distribution unconstrained: genre, length, tone, structure, and level of detail are all wide open, so the output varies a great deal from call to call, because there are many plausible continuations of those three words.

Specificity is about narrowing that space, not about being thorough or polite. It also isn't the same as length: a short prompt that names the audience, format and constraints beats a long one that rambles. Compare 'write about dogs' with 'write a 150-word paragraph for a veterinary clinic's blog, aimed at first-time dog owners, explaining why puppies need multiple rounds of vaccinations rather than just one, in a warm but not overly cute tone, and without using bullet points.' Every clause in the second version removes a swath of plausible continuations (length, audience, topic angle, tone and format are all pinned down), so the range of likely outputs shrinks and repeated calls tend to converge on similar results.

A useful habit: whenever a prompt's output is inconsistent across runs or doesn't match what you wanted, ask which dimension was left unconstrained (length? audience? format? tone? things to exclude?) instead of vaguely 'improving' the wording. Underspecification, not model unreliability, is a very common root cause of inconsistent prompt behavior.

sections.heading: Few-Shot Examples: Showing Instead of Telling
sections.body:
**Few-shot prompting** means including a small number of example input/output pairs directly in the prompt before the actual new input, letting the model infer the desired pattern from those examples rather than (or in addition to) a written instruction. This works for the same reason instructions work: the examples become part of 'everything written so far' that conditions generation, and pattern completion is what the model is built for. Given several examples that follow a pattern, the highest-probability continuation for a new, similar input is to follow it.

```python
prompt = '''Classify the sentiment of each review as positive, negative, or neutral.

Review: "This blender broke after two uses."
Sentiment: negative

Review: "Works exactly as described, very happy with it."
Sentiment: positive

Review: "It's fine, does what it says, nothing special."
Sentiment: neutral

Review: "Fast shipping but the product itself is mediocre."
Sentiment:'''
```

Few-shot examples earn their cost (they use context-window tokens on every call) when the desired format or edge-case handling is hard to describe in words but easy to demonstrate: an unusual output schema, a subtle tone, a tricky boundary between two similar categories. They add little for tasks the model already handles zero-shot, where the extra tokens mostly add cost.

The most common pitfall is **unrepresentative examples**: if every example shares some accidental property (all three sentiment examples above are short, or, worse, all three happen to be non-negative), the model can latch onto that pattern instead of the rule you intended, and mishandle inputs that don't share it. Example order can matter too, and the token cost is recurring, not one-time; weigh both against how much the task benefits from demonstration versus instruction alone. A practical check is to hold out a set of inputs that are not in your examples, run the prompt over them, and see whether swapping or reordering the examples changes the results.

sections.heading: Requesting Structured Output Reliably
Putting It Together: A Layered Prompt
sections.body:
Production prompts are rarely a single sentence. They layer these techniques: a role or system-level instruction that sets overall behavior and tone; the task and its constraints; the output schema or format, ideally with an example; and, when the task benefits from demonstration, a few few-shot examples, usually placed closest to the new input because content nearer the point of generation tends to influence it most.

A common bug in layered prompts is a contradiction across layers that the author misses because each layer looks fine alone: a system prompt that says 'always respond in formal English,' paired with a few-shot example in a casual tone or a different language, gives the model conflicting signals about which pattern to follow, and the result is often an unpredictable blend or a different choice on different calls. When a layered prompt behaves erratically, check every layer against every other for this kind of conflict before assuming the model is unreliable.

examples.title: Specificity Turns a Vague Prompt Into a Reliable One
examples.code:
vague_prompt = "Write about dogs."

specific_prompt = (
    "Write a 150-word paragraph for a veterinary clinic's blog, aimed at "
    "first-time dog owners, explaining why puppies need multiple rounds of "
    "vaccinations rather than just one. Use a warm but professional tone. "
    "Do not use bullet points or headings; plain prose only."
)
examples.explanation: Both prompts are complete instructions, but they leave very different amounts of room. The vague version leaves topic angle, audience, length, tone, and format unconstrained, so the output varies a lot between calls: one run might produce a breed-comparison listicle, another a personal essay, another a set of fun facts. The specific version pins down each of those dimensions, which narrows what counts as a plausible continuation to a smaller, more consistent range. Nothing about the model changed between the two calls, only how much of the output space the prompt left open.

examples.title: Few-Shot Prompting for a Custom Output Style, and the Biased-Example Trap
examples.explanation: The two examples teach a pattern by demonstration: take a plain product description and rewrite it with exclamation points, superlatives, and a direct-address 'your new favorite' framing. The prompt never states that rule in words, because the model infers it from the pattern across both examples. The risk is in how the examples were chosen: both are pleasant, everyday household items rewritten positively. If a new input doesn't fit (a product with a real downside, or a category unlike either example), the model has no demonstrated precedent for handling it, and might force an enthusiastic tone onto something that shouldn't get one, or handle it inconsistently across calls. Good few-shot sets include examples that span the range of cases you expect, not just the easy ones that were convenient to write.

examples.title: Structured Output With Defensive Parsing and a Retry Loop
examples.explanation: Even with `response_format={"type": "json_object"}`, a provider feature rather than a plain-text instruction, the code wraps the parse in a try/except, because 'syntactically valid JSON' and 'the schema and values you need' are different guarantees, and JSON mode only covers the former (and not even that if the output is cut off at the token limit). The retry loop is the more interesting part: instead of failing immediately, it feeds the malformed output and the parser's error message back into the conversation and asks the model to correct it. The error message becomes useful conditioning context for the next attempt, so the model can often see what went wrong (an unescaped quote, a trailing comma) and fix it, which a generic 'try again' with no detail usually can't. Capping retries and raising a clear exception afterward keeps this from looping forever or passing bad data downstream.

misconceptions.description: Being more polite, more verbose, or adding a longer preamble to a prompt ('please', extended context-setting, flattery) makes the model perform noticeably better.
misconceptions.clarification: What improves reliability is narrowing the space of plausible continuations through specificity (constraints, format, audience, examples), not politeness or volume of text. Padding a prompt with pleasantries or preamble adds tokens, which cost money and context budget, without constraining the output, and can dilute the signal by burying the important constraints among filler. Precision of constraint is the lever, not tone or length.

misconceptions.description: If you instruct the model to 'return valid JSON matching this schema,' you can trust that the returned string will always be parseable JSON that matches your schema.
misconceptions.clarification: A plain-text instruction to return JSON is more conditioning, like any other instruction: it strongly influences the output but doesn't hard-constrain it, so the model can still produce malformed JSON, extra prose around it, markdown code fences, or fields not in your schema. Reliability requires either a provider feature (JSON mode, structured outputs, function/tool calling) that restricts which tokens are eligible at each step, or defensive parsing with a validate-and-retry loop on your side, ideally both, since JSON mode typically guarantees valid syntax without guaranteeing your schema or correct values.

exercises.prompt: This function asks the model to return JSON and then parses it directly. It works in some test calls but throws json.JSONDecodeError intermittently in production. Find the likely cause and fix the parsing so it handles the model's actual output reliably.
exercises.code:
# fragment: assumes an initialised OpenAI-style `client`
import json

def get_extracted_fields(prompt, client):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt + "\n\nReturn the result as JSON."}],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)   # fails intermittently
hints: A plain-text instruction to 'return the result as JSON' doesn't hard-constrain the output -- what else might the model wrap around the JSON, especially in a chat-style response?
Try printing `raw` the next time this fails -- models often wrap JSON in a markdown code fence (```json ... ```) or add a short sentence before or after it.
Consider two complementary fixes: stripping markdown fences or extra text before parsing, and using a provider's JSON-mode or structured-output parameter instead of relying on instruction text alone.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code relies on a plain-text instruction ('Return the result as JSON') with no hard constraint and no defensive handling, so on calls where the model wraps the JSON in a markdown code fence or adds a leading or trailing sentence (common for a chat-tuned model), `json.loads` receives text that isn't pure JSON and throws. The fix does two independent things. It switches to the `response_format` JSON-mode parameter, a stronger guarantee of valid syntax than instruction text alone (the prompt must still mention JSON, or the API rejects the request). And it strips common wrapping artifacts such as markdown fences before parsing, raising an informative exception that includes the raw text if parsing still fails, instead of letting a bare `JSONDecodeError` propagate with no context. The fence stripping is belt and braces once JSON mode is on, but it costs nothing and covers providers or models without that feature.

exercises.prompt: A few-shot sentiment classifier is built with three example reviews, and all three happen to be positive or neutral -- none are negative. Predict what's likely to happen when a clearly negative new review is classified, and explain why, in terms of what few-shot prompting actually does.
exercises.code:
prompt = '''Classify the sentiment of each review as positive, negative, or neutral.

Review: "Absolutely love this, best purchase this year!"
Sentiment: positive

Review: "It's okay, does the job."
Sentiment: neutral

Review: "Pretty good quality for the price."
Sentiment: positive

Review: "This is the worst product I have ever bought, complete waste of money."
Sentiment:'''
hints: Few-shot prompting works by pattern completion -- the model infers a pattern from the examples it's shown, not from a rule stated anywhere in words.
All three demonstrated examples land on positive or neutral. Has the prompt actually shown the model what a negative example, or the boundary into negative territory, looks like?
Consider: is it more likely the model correctly generalizes to a category it was never shown an example of, or that it's biased toward the labels it has seen repeatedly?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The skewed examples raise the risk of misclassification or inconsistent labels across repeated calls, because none of the three examples shows what a negative classification looks like in this pattern. The prompt demonstrates positive and neutral but gives the model no in-context precedent for negative. A blatantly negative review like this one will often still come out negative from a capable model, because pretraining taught it sentiment and the instruction names the label, so the skew bites hardest on borderline or mixed reviews, and one correct answer doesn't show the prompt is sound.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Few-shot prompting conditions the model on the pattern shown in the examples, and the model has no rule-based understanding of 'positive/negative/neutral' beyond what the prompt demonstrates plus whatever it learned about sentiment in training. Because every example here is positive or neutral, the in-context pattern is skewed (a documented effect often called majority label bias), and the negative review is the first case with no analogous example, so the model falls back on general knowledge of sentiment. For a blatant case that usually works; for borderline cases it can produce inconsistent or miscalibrated labels. The fix is to include at least one clearly negative example, ideally unambiguous, so the demonstrated pattern spans all three labels, and ideally to test on mixed and borderline reviews as well as clear ones.

assessments.prompt: A prompt asks a model to 'return the extracted fields as JSON.' Which statement about the reliability of this instruction is most accurate?
options: It's just additional conditioning text like any other instruction.
It's a hard guarantee -- the API will refuse to return anything other than valid JSON once JSON is explicitly requested in the instructions.
It only works if the prompt also includes at least five few-shot examples of valid JSON output.
JSON requests are handled by a separate, non-generative subsystem that validates syntax before the response is returned to you.
assessments.explanation: A plain-text instruction to return JSON influences generation like any other instruction, by conditioning the probability distribution, but it doesn't hard-constrain which tokens can be produced, so malformed output, wrapping prose, or markdown fences remain possible. Reliability comes from combining it with a provider feature (JSON mode, structured outputs, function calling) and defensive parsing on the calling side. The “It's a hard guarantee -- the API…” option overstates what plain instructions guarantee. The “It only works if the prompt also…” option is false: examples can help, but there's no fixed minimum, and examples alone still don't hard-constrain output. The “JSON requests are handled by a separate…” option is wrong because no validating subsystem sits between generation and the response by default; validation has to be added through a provider's structured-output feature or your own code.

assessments.prompt: A colleague's prompt for extracting structured data from support tickets works reliably in testing but occasionally returns invalid or incomplete JSON in production, at low but nonzero frequency. Explain the likely underlying causes and how you'd make the pipeline robust against this, rather than just hoping it stops happening.
assessments.modelAnswer: A chat-tuned model generating JSON is doing ordinary next-token generation, not running a syntax-checked serialization routine, so 'usually correct' rather than 'always correct' is the expected baseline for JSON from a plain-text instruction, and low-frequency failures are what that predicts: an occasional code fence, a dropped closing brace, a hallucinated or missing field, a number rendered as a quoted string. Testing under-samples this because manual tests reuse a few representative inputs, while production traffic eventually surfaces unusual characters, very long text, and edge-case categories that trigger rarer failures. To make the pipeline robust, don't rely on the instruction text alone. First, switch to a provider feature if one exists (JSON mode, structured outputs, or function/tool calling), which restricts the model to emitting valid JSON instead of just asking. Second, parse defensively downstream: wrap the parse in error handling and strip common wrapping artifacts like markdown fences. For extraction tasks like this one, a low temperature also helps keep the output format stable across calls. Third, validate the parsed result against your required schema (right fields, right types), not just 'is this valid JSON,' since valid JSON can still be missing required data. Fourth, add a bounded retry that feeds the specific parsing or validation error back to the model, which tends to succeed far more often than giving up or retrying blindly. None of this makes failures impossible, but it turns a rare unhandled crash into a monitored, recoverable, measurable failure rate.

assessments.prompt: Why does the vague prompt 'write about dogs' tend to produce noticeably different output across repeated calls, according to this module's explanation of specificity?
options: Because the tokenizer randomly reorders the words in short, vague prompts before encoding them.

Because the prompt leaves many dimensions -- topic angle, length, tone, audience, format -- entirely unconstrained, so many different continuations remain comparably plausible, and which one actually gets produced varies from call to call.
Because prompts under a certain word count automatically trigger a higher default temperature setting.
Because the model intentionally injects randomness into short prompts so its responses appear more creative.
assessments.explanation: Specificity works by narrowing the space of plausible next-token continuations; a vague prompt leaves length, audience, tone, structure, and topic angle open, so many different completions are comparably probable and different calls can land on different ones. The “Because the tokenizer randomly reorders the words…” option misattributes the effect to tokenization, which doesn't reorder anything. The “Because prompts under a certain word count…” and “Because the model intentionally injects randomness into…” options invent mechanisms (an automatic temperature bump or intentional randomness injection tied to prompt length); temperature is a setting you choose, not something the model changes based on how vague a prompt is.

assessments.prompt: A few-shot sentiment classifier is given three example reviews, all of which happen to be positive or neutral -- none negative. Per this module, what's the most likely risk when a borderline, mildly negative new review is classified?
options: The model will refuse to produce any label outside the exact three categories demonstrated, including refusing to say 'negative.'
The API call will fail with an error, because at least one example of every possible output label is required for few-shot prompting to function at all.
The model may misclassify the negative review or handle it inconsistently across calls.
The model will still classify it correctly as negative every time, since sentiment categories are well-known independent of which examples happen to be shown.
assessments.explanation: Few-shot prompting conditions the model on the pattern the examples establish, not on a guaranteed understanding of the task; when every example is positive or neutral, the demonstrated pattern is skewed too, and the model has no in-context precedent for what a negative classification looks like here. The “The model will still classify it correctly…” option wrongly assumes general knowledge always overrides a biased demonstrated pattern. The “The API call will fail…” and “The model will refuse to produce any…” options describe a hard error or an outright refusal, which unrepresentative examples don't cause; the actual risk is quiet misclassification or inconsistency.

assessments.prompt: A layered prompt's system message instructs 'always respond in formal English,' but a few-shot example included lower in that same prompt is written in a casual tone. Per this module, what's the likely result?
options: The model detects the contradiction explicitly and pauses generation to ask the user which instruction should take priority.
The system-level instruction always wins outright, since it appears earlier in the prompt, so the casual example has no effect on the output.
The few-shot example always overrides the system instruction, since content closer to the point of generation always wins entirely.
The two layers hand the model genuinely conflicting conditioning signals.
assessments.explanation: Contradictions across prompt layers are a common bug because each layer looks fine alone, but together they leave the model with conflicting signals about which pattern to follow, typically producing an unpredictable blend or inconsistent choice rather than either layer cleanly winning. The “The system-level instruction always wins outright, since…” and “The few-shot example always overrides the system…” options both assume one layer completely overrides the other; position alone doesn't guarantee dominance. The “The model detects the contradiction explicitly…” option describes a clarifying-question behavior that isn't part of the base generation mechanism; the model doesn't pause to resolve conflicting instructions on its own.

concepts.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, End to End
concepts.description: RAG addresses two problems with relying on a model's trained-in knowledge, information that's stale, private, or never seen and answers that can't be traced to a source, by retrieving relevant text at query time and feeding it into the context window as grounding for generation.
learningObjectives: Describe the end-to-end RAG pipeline: chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, augmentation, and generation, and what each stage is responsible for.
Explain the chunk-size tradeoff between retrieval precision and preserved context, and why fixed-size chunking is a starting point rather than a final answer.
Explain what an embedding and vector similarity search compute conceptually, and when semantic search underperforms exact keyword matching.
Diagnose common RAG failure modes -- irrelevant retrieved chunks, ungrounded answers, boundary-cut context -- and identify which pipeline stage is responsible.
Explain why RAG substantially reduces but does not eliminate hallucination, tying the explanation back to the underlying generation mechanism.

sections.heading: The End-to-End Pipeline
sections.body:
RAG is a pipeline of independently tunable stages, and most RAG debugging is isolating which stage is underperforming instead of treating 'the RAG system' as one thing to fix. **Ingestion and chunking** splits source documents into passages small enough to be individually retrievable and to comfortably co-exist with several other chunks in a single prompt. **Embedding** converts each chunk's text into a dense numeric vector, produced by a separate embedding model, that's meant to capture the chunk's semantic content -- similar meanings should land at nearby points in that vector space. **Indexing** stores those vectors (usually alongside the original chunk text and metadata) in a structure -- often called a vector database or vector index -- built for fast nearest-neighbor search over potentially millions of vectors. Storing metadata with each chunk (source document, section, last-updated date) is what later lets you filter results and show citations. **Retrieval** happens at query time: the incoming user query is embedded with the same embedding model, and the index is searched for the chunks whose vectors are most similar to the query's vector, returning the top-k matches. Queries and chunks must be embedded with the same model; switching embedding models means re-embedding the whole corpus. **Augmentation** inserts the text of those retrieved chunks into the prompt sent to the generation model, typically alongside instructions about how to use them. **Generation** then produces the final answer, conditioned on both the original question and the injected context.

Each of these six stages can fail independently, and a poor answer can trace back to any of them: bad chunking, a mismatched embedding model, a misconfigured index, retrieval returning irrelevant matches, weak augmentation instructions, or the generation model ignoring good context. Don't assume the fix is always 'get a better generation model'; find the stage first. It is the most useful debugging habit for these systems.

sections.heading: Chunking: A Design Decision That Gets Underrated
sections.body:
Chunk size is an unavoidable tradeoff, and usually the first thing worth tuning when a RAG system underperforms. Chunks that are **too large** dilute the relevance signal used in retrieval: a chunk with one relevant sentence buried in several paragraphs of unrelated text gets a weaker, blended similarity score than a tightly relevant short chunk, so it can rank below chunks that are less useful. Large chunks also mean fewer distinct chunks fit in your context budget, so fewer independently relevant pieces of information per query. Chunks that are **too small**, on the other hand, lose the surrounding context a fragment needs to be individually meaningful -- a chunk containing just 'the deadline is March 3rd' with no sentence establishing what deadline is being discussed is close to useless once retrieved in isolation -- and they multiply the total number of vectors in your index, which increases both storage and retrieval latency.

**Overlap** between consecutive chunks (having each chunk share, say, the last 10-20% of its text with the next chunk) is the standard mitigation for an important sentence landing on a chunk boundary and getting split across two chunks, neither of which contains the complete thought, at the cost of some redundant storage. As a general practice, chunk boundaries that respect a document's natural structure (paragraph breaks, section headers) tend to outperform boundaries chosen purely by a fixed character or token count, because natural boundaries are more likely to be semantic boundaries. Fixed-size chunking is a reasonable starting point, not a technique to stop iterating on once it works. Sizes are usually set in tokens rather than characters, because the embedding model's input limit and your prompt budget are both counted in tokens. Always look at a sample of the actual chunks your splitter produces; chunks that start mid-sentence or split a table from its header are easy to spot and expensive to ignore.

sections.heading: Embeddings and Vector Similarity Search
sections.body:
An **embedding model** is a separate, typically much smaller model trained specifically to map a piece of text to a point in a high-dimensional vector space, such that text with similar meaning ends up at nearby points and text with different meaning ends up farther apart. Similarity between two vectors is usually measured with cosine similarity or a dot product, and 'retrieval' at query time is fundamentally the operation 'find the k stored vectors nearest to this query's vector.'

The practical power of this approach, relative to classic keyword search (like BM25 or a plain text index), is that it captures semantic relatedness rather than lexical overlap -- a query about 'automobile maintenance' can retrieve a chunk about 'car servicing' even though the two share almost no words in common, because an embedding model trained on enough text learns that those phrases mean similar things. But this has a cost that's often underestimated: semantic search can underperform exact keyword matching for queries where the exact string matters -- a specific error code, a product SKU, a person's name, a precise legal term -- because two vectors can be semantically 'close' in a general sense while still failing to prioritize an exact match strongly enough, and the embedding model may not have learned fine-grained distinctions between similar-looking codes or identifiers it saw rarely (or never) during its own training. That's why many production retrieval systems are **hybrid**: they combine semantic vector search with traditional keyword search (and often a separate reranking step that re-scores the combined candidate set with a more precise, more expensive model), rather than relying on embeddings alone. Merging the two result lists is its own design choice; reciprocal rank fusion, which scores each result by its rank in each list, is a common simple option.

sections.heading: Augmentation and Generation: Why Grounding Instructions Matter
sections.body:
Pasting retrieved chunk text into the prompt is not enough, by itself, to ground the model's answer in it. The generation model still has its trained-in knowledge conditioning every token alongside the text you injected, and without instruction there's a risk that it blends the two, or sometimes favors its own (possibly outdated or wrong) belief over the retrieved text. Augmentation instructions such as 'answer only using the context provided below; if the answer is not contained in the context, say you don't know rather than guessing' shift generation toward using the retrieved material as the primary source, instead of treating it as one more loosely relevant text alongside everything the model already 'knows.' Mark where the context starts and ends (with delimiters or tags), and remember that retrieved text can itself contain instructions, for example a document that says 'ignore previous instructions.' Treat it as data to answer from, not as commands, and say so in the prompt.

```python
system_prompt = (
    "Answer the user's question using ONLY the context below. "
    "If the answer is not present in the context, say you don't know -- "
    "do not use outside knowledge or guess.\n\nContext:\n" + retrieved_context
)
```

Two failure modes to watch for are near mirror images: a model that ignores good, correctly retrieved context in favor of its own prior belief (usually fixable with a firmer grounding instruction), and a model that answers confidently from irrelevant context because retrieval returned a poor match (a retrieval-stage bug that no augmentation instruction can fix, since the model can't be grounded in relevant text it was never given).

sections.heading: Why RAG Reduces But Doesn't Eliminate Hallucination
sections.body:
RAG reduces hallucination in practice, and the mechanism follows from what you know about generation: injecting relevant, verified text into the context narrows the space of plausible continuations toward content grounded in that text, as any conditioning does. It is among the most effective hallucination mitigations available.

But generation is still the same underlying probabilistic mechanism as always, and RAG doesn't change that. If retrieval returns irrelevant or wrong chunks, you've grounded the model in the wrong material and it can still generate a confident answer from it: garbage in, confidently phrased garbage out, indistinguishable to the model from the case where the material was correct. If the retrieved context is ambiguous or incomplete, the model may fill gaps with its own assumptions instead of flagging the ambiguity. And even with good, unambiguous context, the model can occasionally blend it with prior beliefs or misread a nuance. RAG changes the odds substantially in your favor, but it cannot reduce the risk to zero, because the final answer is still produced token by token by the same mechanism.

examples.title: A Minimal RAG Pipeline, Stage by Stage
examples.code:
def build_index(documents, chunk_size=500, overlap=50):
    chunks = []
    for doc in documents:
        chunks.extend(split_into_chunks(doc.text, chunk_size, overlap))
    vectors = [embed(chunk) for chunk in chunks]         # embedding stage
    return VectorIndex(vectors, chunks)                   # indexing stage

def answer_question(question, index, generation_model, top_k=4):
    query_vector = embed(question)
    retrieved = index.search(query_vector, top_k=top_k)   # retrieval stage
    context_text = "\n\n---\n\n".join(chunk.text for chunk in retrieved)
    prompt = (
        "Answer using ONLY the context below. If the answer isn't present, "
        "say you don't know.\n\nContext:\n" + context_text +
        "\n\nQuestion: " + question
    )
    return generation_model.generate(prompt)               # augmentation + generation stages

index = build_index(company_docs)
print(answer_question("What is the refund window for annual plans?", index, model))
examples.explanation: Each call maps onto one pipeline stage: `split_into_chunks` and `embed` inside `build_index` handle chunking and embedding, `VectorIndex` handles indexing, `index.search` handles retrieval, and the prompt construction plus `generation_model.generate` handle augmentation and generation. (This is a sketch: `split_into_chunks`, `embed`, `VectorIndex`, `company_docs` and `model` are placeholders for your own components.) When the pipeline gives a wrong answer, the question is 'which stage,' not 'is the model bad.' Print `retrieved` to check that retrieval found relevant chunks before suspecting generation; inspect `chunks` right after `build_index` to check that chunking produced sensible, self-contained passages; and only once retrieval returns relevant material is it worth working on the augmentation instructions or the generation model.

examples.title: Chunk Size Changes What Gets Retrieved
examples.code:
source_paragraph = (
    "Annual plan subscribers may request a full refund within 30 days of "
    "purchase. Monthly plan subscribers are not eligible for refunds but may "
    "cancel at any time to stop future charges. All refund requests must be "
    "submitted through the billing portal, not by email."
)

# Chunked as ONE large chunk (the whole paragraph):
# -> A query "how do monthly subscribers cancel" retrieves this whole chunk;
#    it contains the answer, but diluted alongside two unrelated refund rules.

# Chunked into THREE smaller, sentence-level chunks:
# -> chunk 1: "Annual plan subscribers may request a full refund within 30 days of purchase."
# -> chunk 2: "Monthly plan subscribers are not eligible for refunds but may cancel at any time to stop future charges."
# -> chunk 3: "All refund requests must be submitted through the billing portal, not by email."
# -> The same query now retrieves chunk 2 specifically, a tight, relevant match.
examples.explanation: This illustrates the chunk-size tradeoff. The large chunk isn't wrong, since the answer is in it, but it tends to score as a weaker, more diluted match than a chunk that is purely about the query topic, because its embedding has to represent three different pieces of information blended together. (The retrieval results in the comments are illustrative; real scores depend on the embedding model.) The sentence-level chunk's embedding is almost entirely about the thing being asked, which tends to rank higher and gives the generation model cleaner context instead of making it pick the right sentence out of a mixed passage. The tradeoff not shown here is that chunks this small can lose broader context in other cases; a real system usually lands between single sentences and whole documents, tuned against real queries.

examples.title: Grounding Instructions Change Whether Retrieved Context Actually Gets Used
examples.code:
retrieved_context = "Refunds for annual plans are available within 30 days of purchase."

weak_prompt = f"Context: {retrieved_context}\n\nQuestion: What is the refund policy?"

strong_prompt = (
    f"Answer the question using ONLY the context below. If the answer is not "
    f"in the context, say you don't know rather than guessing.\n\n"
    f"Context: {retrieved_context}\n\nQuestion: What is the refund policy?"
)
examples.explanation: Both prompts contain the same retrieved context but put very different pressure on how it gets used. The weak version presents the context and question side by side with no instruction about their relationship, so the model infers how strictly to stick to the text versus supplementing it with general knowledge about refund policies from training, and different calls can resolve that differently. The strong version tells the model to treat the context as the sole source of truth and to decline rather than guess when the context is insufficient, which makes it more likely that the answer traces back to the retrieved text rather than to a generic assumption about how refund policies 'usually' work. Neither version guarantees grounding, but the instruction shifts the odds substantially, which is why production RAG prompts nearly always include one. Asking the model to quote or cite the passage it used makes unsupported answers easier to spot, and a short test set of questions whose answers are not in the corpus shows whether it really says 'I don't know.'

misconceptions.description: Once RAG is added to a system, the model can no longer hallucinate, because it's effectively just looking up and returning the answer from a database rather than generating it.
misconceptions.clarification: RAG only changes what text is available in the context the model conditions on. Generation is still the same probabilistic, token-by-token mechanism, drawing on both the injected context and the model's trained-in knowledge. If retrieval returns irrelevant or wrong chunks, the model can still generate a confident, fluent, ungrounded answer from that bad material; if the retrieved context is ambiguous, the model can still fill the gap with an assumption rather than flagging uncertainty. RAG substantially reduces hallucination risk in practice, but it shifts the odds; it isn't a non-generative mechanism that makes fabrication impossible.

misconceptions.description: Bigger chunks -- or feeding whole documents instead of chunking at all -- are always better, because the model has 'more context to work with.'
misconceptions.clarification: Larger chunks dilute the relevance signal that similarity search relies on: a long chunk containing one relevant sentence amid several irrelevant ones scores as a weaker match than a short chunk that's tightly about the query topic, which can cause genuinely useful material to rank below less useful material during retrieval. Larger chunks also mean fewer distinct, independently-relevant pieces of information fit within your context budget for a given query. Chunk size trades retrieval precision against preserved surrounding context; neither 'bigger is better' nor 'smaller is better' holds.

exercises.prompt: This RAG function retrieves relevant chunks but the model's answers never actually reflect the retrieved content -- they read like generic, ungrounded responses. Find the bug.
hints: Trace `context_text` after it's built -- is it actually included anywhere in the string that gets sent to `generation_model.generate`?
Retrieval can work perfectly while augmentation, the step that injects those chunks into the prompt, fails to do so. Check which stage this bug lives in.
The fix isn't about retrieval quality; it's about including `context_text` inside the `prompt` string, along with an instruction telling the model to use it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Retrieval works as intended (`retrieved` and `context_text` are computed correctly), but augmentation never happens: `context_text` is built and then discarded, since the `prompt` sent to the model contains only the question. It shows why RAG debugging should isolate stages: 'ungrounded answers' suggests a generation or retrieval-quality problem, but here everything through retrieval is fine and the augmentation step was never wired up. The fix interpolates `context_text` into the prompt and adds a grounding instruction, which gives the generation model something to be grounded in.

exercises.prompt: A RAG system retrieves the top 10 chunks for every query with no similarity-score filtering, and it's returning several barely-related chunks alongside the genuinely relevant ones, diluting the context with noise. Write a function filter_by_relevance(retrieved_chunks, min_score) that takes a list of (chunk, similarity_score) tuples and returns only the chunks meeting a minimum similarity threshold, preserving their original relative order.
exercises.code:
def filter_by_relevance(retrieved_chunks, min_score):
    # retrieved_chunks: list of (chunk_text, similarity_score) tuples, already sorted by score descending
    # return: list of chunk_text strings whose similarity_score >= min_score
    pass
hints: This doesn't require re-sorting anything -- the input is already described as sorted by score descending, so a simple filter that preserves order is sufficient.
Watch the off-by-one direction on the comparison: you want to KEEP chunks whose score is at or above the threshold, not strictly above it.
The return type should be a list of just the chunk text strings, not the (chunk, score) tuples -- make sure you're unpacking correctly.
exercises.solutionCode:
def filter_by_relevance(retrieved_chunks, min_score):
    return [chunk for chunk, score in retrieved_chunks if score >= min_score]

# Example:
retrieved = [("Refunds for annual plans...", 0.91), ("Our office hours are...", 0.42), ("Monthly plans cannot be refunded...", 0.86)]
print(filter_by_relevance(retrieved, min_score=0.75))
# ['Refunds for annual plans...', 'Monthly plans cannot be refunded...']
exercises.solutionExplanation: This is a small but important production pattern: top-k retrieval always returns k results whether or not all k are relevant, because 'top-k' means 'the k best matches available,' not 'the matches that are good.' A similarity threshold applied after retrieval and before augmentation drops chunks that barely resemble the query. If fewer than k chunks are relevant, it returns fewer than k (or none) instead of padding the context with noise to hit a fixed count. In a real system `min_score` needs tuning against representative queries, since the right threshold depends on which embedding model produced the scores and how your corpus is distributed in that vector space (scores from different embedding models aren't comparable).

assessments.prompt: A support bot using RAG confidently answers a question with information that sounds plausible but is actually about an unrelated product from the indexed documents. Retrieval logs show the top-k chunks it was given were all genuinely about that unrelated product. Which stage of the pipeline is the most likely root cause?
options: The generation model, which should be replaced with a larger model.
The tokenizer, which likely mis-split the user's question.
The augmentation stage, because grounding instructions can't fix irrelevant retrieved content in the first place.
The retrieval stage -- the query embedding matched chunks that were not actually relevant to the user's question.
assessments.explanation: The logs show the retrieved chunks were about the wrong product, so the model did what a well-grounded generation step should: it answered from the context it was given. The failure happened earlier, in retrieval, which returned the wrong chunks; no generation-model behavior or grounding instruction can produce a correct answer from context about the wrong topic. The “The generation model, which should be replaced…” option misdiagnoses a retrieval problem as a generation-capability problem. The “The augmentation stage, because grounding instructions can't…” option sounds reasonable but is wrong: augmentation instructions govern how retrieved context is used, not whether the right context was retrieved, so augmentation is not the root cause here (though it's true instructions can't fix it after the fact). The “The tokenizer, which likely mis-split the user's question” option is implausible on the evidence given; nothing here points to a tokenization failure.

assessments.prompt: Explain why a RAG-based chatbot might confidently give a wrong answer to a question even though the correct information genuinely exists somewhere in the indexed document set, walking through where in the pipeline this could go wrong.
assessments.modelAnswer: The correct information existing in the corpus only helps if every later stage carries it through to the final answer, and the chain can break at several independent points. The problem could originate in chunking, if the correct information was split awkwardly across a chunk boundary, leaving no single chunk that contains the complete, coherent answer, or if it was embedded inside a large chunk dominated by unrelated content, weakening its similarity score. It could originate in retrieval itself, if the query's embedding simply doesn't land close enough to the correct chunk's embedding in vector space -- this happens especially when the question uses very different wording from the source, or when the answer depends on an exact match (an ID, a specific term) that semantic search handles less reliably than keyword search. It could originate in augmentation, if the retrieved chunks are correct but the prompt lacks a firm grounding instruction, leaving room for the model to blend in its own assumptions. And even if retrieval and augmentation worked, generation can still misread, oversimplify, or blend a nuance of the correct text with something else, since it's ordinary next-token prediction. To find out which happened, inspect each stage instead of guessing; checking what was retrieved for the failing query is usually the fastest first step, since many RAG failures turn out to be retrieval failures rather than generation failures.

assessments.prompt: A chunk contains the correct answer sentence buried among several unrelated sentences. A smaller, tightly-relevant chunk about only the query topic exists elsewhere in the index. Per this module, why does the larger chunk often rank below the smaller one during similarity search, even though it technically contains the answer?
options: Vector indexes silently truncate long chunks before embedding them, so part of the answer is dropped before indexing even happens.

The larger chunk's embedding represents an average of several different pieces of content, diluting the specific relevance signal, so it scores as a weaker match than a chunk that's purely about the query's topic.
Larger chunks are always processed by a separate, lower-quality embedding model reserved for bulk content.
Vector databases apply a fixed length-based score penalty to any chunk over a certain character count.
assessments.explanation: A large chunk's embedding has to represent several different pieces of information blended together, which weakens its similarity score relative to a chunk tightly focused on the query topic. The “Vector databases apply a fixed length-based score…”, “Vector indexes silently truncate long chunks before…”, and “Larger chunks are always processed…” options each invent a mechanism (a fixed length penalty, silent truncation, or a separate lower-quality model for large chunks); the effect is about how blending diverse content into one embedding dilutes its relevance signal. (Embedding models do have maximum input lengths, and text past the limit can be truncated, but that is a separate matter from ranking.)

assessments.prompt: A user searches a RAG-indexed support knowledge base for a specific product SKU code. Per this module, why might pure semantic vector search underperform plain keyword search for this particular kind of query?
options: Two vectors can be semantically 'close' in a general sense without the embedding model having learned fine-grained distinctions between similar-looking exact identifiers, so an exact match may not be prioritized as strongly as it should be.
Vector databases cannot store or index strings containing numeric characters, so SKU codes are dropped entirely.
Semantic embedding models only function on queries phrased as complete grammatical sentences, not short codes.
Keyword search is unconditionally more accurate than semantic search for every query type, which is why hybrid retrieval is never actually necessary.
assessments.explanation: Exact strings such as error codes, SKUs, names, and precise legal terms are a case where semantic similarity can underperform lexical matching, because the embedding model may not have learned fine-grained distinctions between similar-looking rare identifiers, even though it captures broader relatedness well. The “Vector databases cannot store or index strings…” and “Semantic embedding models only function on queries…” options describe technical limitations that don't exist. The “Keyword search is unconditionally more accurate…” option overstates the case the other way: hybrid systems are common because neither approach wins on every query type.

assessments.prompt: Which statement best reflects why this module says RAG substantially reduces, but structurally cannot eliminate, hallucination?
options: RAG only reduces hallucination when the generation model's temperature is set above 1.0.
RAG fails to reduce hallucination at all, because vector databases are inherently less reliable than relational databases.

Generation is still the same token-by-token probabilistic mechanism as always; if retrieval returns wrong or irrelevant chunks the model can still confidently generate an answer from that bad material, and even good, relevant context can occasionally get blended with the model's own prior beliefs.
RAG eliminates hallucination completely, because a grounded model can only copy retrieved text verbatim into its final answer.
assessments.explanation: RAG narrows the space of plausible continuations toward grounded content, which substantially helps, but generation remains the same probabilistic mechanism: bad retrieval still produces confidently phrased garbage, and even correct retrieved context can be blended with or overridden by the model's trained-in assumptions. The “RAG eliminates hallucination completely, because a grounded…” option overstates the guarantee retrieval provides. The “RAG fails to reduce hallucination at all…” option mischaracterizes RAG as providing no benefit at all, which contradicts the evidence that it's one of the most effective mitigations available. The “RAG only reduces hallucination when the generation…” option invents a dependency on a temperature threshold that doesn't exist.

assessments.prompt: A support chatbot built with RAG confidently gives an outdated refund policy even though the policy document was updated last week. Walk through how you would find and fix the cause.
assessments.modelAnswer: Separate retrieval from generation. First check the index: was the updated document re-ingested, and were the old chunks deleted or overwritten? Ingestion that only appends leaves both versions searchable, and the old one may rank higher. Then inspect what was retrieved for this question: log the retrieved chunks and scores. If the old chunk wins, fix ingestion to upsert by stable document ID, delete stale chunks, and store metadata like updated_at so you can filter or prefer recent versions. If the right chunk is retrieved but ignored, tighten the prompt to answer only from provided context and cite the source, or add reranking. Finally add this question to a golden evaluation set with the expected answer, and run retrieval and answer checks whenever documents or prompts change so regressions are caught before users see them.

concepts.title: Fine-Tuning vs RAG vs Prompting: Choosing the Right Tool
concepts.description: Fine-tuning, RAG, and prompting change three different things (model weights, available context, and per-call instructions, respectively), and confusing them leads teams to fine-tune a knowledge problem that RAG would have solved in an afternoon, or to prompt-engineer around a behavior gap that only training data can close.
learningObjectives: Distinguish what fine-tuning changes (model weights and default behavior) from what RAG changes (available context per call) and what prompting changes (per-call instructions).
Classify a given problem as primarily a knowledge problem, a behavior/format problem, or a specification problem, and match it to the right tool.
Explain the cost, latency, and maintenance tradeoffs across prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning.
Explain why fine-tuning is a poor fix for factual or frequently-changing knowledge, and why RAG is a poor fix for consistent style, tone, or format shifts.
Design a layered strategy for a realistic product scenario that combines prompting and RAG first, reaching for fine-tuning only when justified by data and scale.

sections.heading: Three Different Levers for Three Different Problems
sections.body:
The three techniques are easy to conflate in casual conversation, but they do different things. **Prompting** changes per-call instructions. It's the cheapest and fastest to iterate on, changes nothing persistent about the model, and every effect disappears when you stop including the instruction. **RAG** changes what's available in the context for a given call, by retrieving and injecting external, often frequently changing or private information at inference time. It also leaves the weights and default behavior alone; it gives the model different material to condition on. **Fine-tuning** is additional training that adjusts the model's weights, which persistently shifts its default behavior, tone, or narrow-task performance without repeating an instruction on every call.

The consequence: these are usually not three competing solutions to one problem that you pick between on preference or budget. They answer three different questions -- 'what do I want the model to know for this specific call' (RAG), 'what do I want to tell it to do right now' (prompting), and 'what do I want it to always, persistently do or be good at, without being told again each time' (fine-tuning). Treating them as interchangeable is the root of most of the mismatched-tool mistakes below.

sections.heading: When Fine-Tuning Is the Right Tool
sections.body:
Fine-tuning earns its cost and complexity in a few recurring situations. First, when you need a specific output format or style reproduced very consistently across a high volume of calls, and carrying a long instruction-plus-few-shot block in every prompt is itself becoming a cost. Fine-tuning bakes the pattern into the weights, so the prompt no longer re-explains it, saving tokens (and therefore cost and latency) at scale. Second, when you're teaching a narrow behavior or classification boundary that's hard to specify in words but easy to demonstrate with many labeled examples (a subtle tone distinction, a nuanced categorization with many edge cases), where the number of examples needed exceeds what fits as few-shot examples in one prompt. Third, when the base model handles your input distribution poorly (heavy domain jargon, an unusual input format, a language variety it saw little of) and prompting can't close the gap because the limitation is in the model's representations, not in what it's been told.

Each of these has prerequisites and costs. You need a reasonably large, high-quality, representative labeled dataset (a small or biased dataset produces a narrow or biased fine-tune). The iteration loop is slow and expensive compared with editing a prompt, and checking that a new fine-tune improved things without degrading other capabilities takes effort. And a poorly executed fine-tune can make the model regress on tasks it handled before, sometimes called catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning is not a low-risk, low-cost lever the way changing a prompt is. It also ties you to a specific base model: when you move to a newer base model, you generally have to repeat the fine-tune, whereas a prompt or a retrieval index usually carries over with little change.

sections.heading: When Fine-Tuning Is the Wrong Tool
sections.body:
A very common fine-tuning misapplication is using it to inject **knowledge** (facts, current data, a company's internal documentation) in the hope that the model will then reliably recall it on demand. It doesn't work the way people expect: fine-tuning adjusts weights in a diffuse, statistical way across training, and it is not a reliable way to get a model to recall a specific fact verbatim, especially one that appeared only a few times in the fine-tuning data. The same probabilistic generation mechanism that causes hallucination in the base model governs a fine-tuned model too. Fine-tuning shifts the distribution; it doesn't install a lookup table, so the model can paraphrase, blend, or forget a fine-tuned fact as easily as recall it precisely.

There's also a freshness and traceability problem that's arguably worse in practice. Any fact baked into fine-tuning weights goes stale when the real-world information changes, and fixing that takes another retraining cycle, slow and expensive compared with re-indexing an updated document for RAG, which takes minutes. And a fine-tuned model's answer, even when correct, can't show *which source* it came from, whereas a RAG answer can point at the retrieved passage that supports it. For a 'the model needs to know X' requirement where X is factual, sourced, or changing, RAG is the cheaper, more reliable, more traceable tool, even when budget for fine-tuning isn't a constraint, because the limitation is mechanical, not financial.

sections.heading: The Decision in Practice
sections.body:
A heuristic to run through before committing engineering effort to any one approach: if the core problem is 'the model doesn't know something,' 'this information changes regularly,' or 'we need to be able to trace an answer back to a source,' that's a knowledge problem, and RAG is the right lever regardless of budget. If the core problem is 'the model does know how to do this, but I need it to consistently behave a specific way on every single call, re-explaining that behavior every time is expensive or produces inconsistent results, and we have a large, clean set of examples of exactly the behavior we want,' that's a fine-tuning candidate, but try prompting and few-shot examples first, since they're nearly free to test and often close enough of the gap that fine-tuning turns out to be unnecessary. If the core problem is 'I need to phrase this feature's instructions more precisely, or show a couple of examples of the format I want,' that's a prompting problem, and reaching for RAG or fine-tuning would solve a problem you don't have.

Most real systems layer these: start with prompting because it's nearly free to iterate on, add RAG once there's a knowledge, freshness, or traceability need, and reach for fine-tuning only once prompting and RAG together have hit a ceiling on a specific, reproducible behavior gap and there's a labeled dataset to train on. Fine-tuning as a first move is very often solving the wrong problem, or solving the right one with the most expensive, slowest tool.

sections.heading: A Layered Example
sections.body:
Consider an internal support-ticket triage assistant that needs to categorize incoming tickets, cite the relevant internal policy for its categorization decision, and output a consistent structured format for downstream automation. Build it in layers. Start with **prompting**: a clear system instruction describing the categories, the required output schema, and a couple of few-shot examples of well-formed classifications; this alone often gets a working first version. Add **RAG** once the assistant needs to reference current internal policy documents to justify its categorization and those documents change periodically. Retrieving the relevant policy section per ticket and citing it solves both knowledge freshness and traceability without touching model weights.

Only later, if ticket volume is high enough that the per-call cost of the few-shot examples and schema instructions becomes a meaningful expense, and production traffic has produced a large, clean dataset of human-verified classifications, does fine-tuning become worth considering. It would bake in the output formatting (which doesn't change over time) so it no longer needs re-specifying in every prompt, while retrieval keeps handling the policy knowledge (which does change) as before. The two techniques solve different halves of the same system, and neither should be asked to solve the half it's ill-suited for.

examples.title: The Wrong-Tool Attempt: Fine-Tuning on Policy Text
examples.code:
# Attempt: fine-tune a model on a dataset built from the company's internal
# policy documents, hoping it will then reliably answer policy questions
# and cite the right policy.

training_examples = [
    {"prompt": "What is the refund window for annual plans?",
     "completion": "Annual plan subscribers may request a full refund within 30 days of purchase, per Section 4.2 of the Refund Policy."},
    # ... hundreds more examples generated from policy documents ...
]

# fine_tune(base_model, training_examples)  -- weeks later, in production:
# The policy changes (30 days -> 45 days). The fine-tuned model keeps
# confidently citing "30 days" and "Section 4.2" until it is retrained
# on an updated dataset -- a slow, costly cycle to repeat every time policy changes.
examples.explanation: This looks reasonable on paper: there's training data, and the model will probably learn to answer some policy questions correctly right after fine-tuning. The failure shows up over time. When the policy changes, the fine-tuned model has no way to know, because the fact is baked statistically into its weights rather than looked up each time, and it keeps citing the outdated number, with a section reference that adds false credibility, until someone notices, rebuilds the dataset, and pays for another fine-tuning run. This is the freshness and traceability problem from the explanation: the fix isn't a better fine-tuning dataset but recognizing that factual, changeable information belongs in a retrieval index that can be updated in minutes, not in weights that need a retraining cycle.

examples.title: A Case Where Fine-Tuning Actually Wins
examples.code:
# A classification pipeline processes 2 million support tickets per month.
# The current prompt includes a lengthy instruction block plus 8 few-shot
# examples to enforce a specific, consistent structured-output format --
# roughly 900 extra tokens on EVERY call, just to establish format
# and tone, which never change from ticket to ticket.

cost_per_1k_tokens = 0.01   # illustrative price in dollars; check your provider's current rates
extra_tokens_per_call = 900
calls_per_month = 2_000_000

monthly_cost_of_repeated_instructions = (
    extra_tokens_per_call / 1000 * cost_per_1k_tokens * calls_per_month
)
print(monthly_cost_of_repeated_instructions)   # roughly $18,000/month, just for repeated formatting instructions

# There is also a large (50,000+), clean, human-verified dataset of past
# correctly classified tickets available from production history, and the
# desired formatting behavior doesn't change over time.
examples.explanation: This is close to the ideal fine-tuning scenario: the behavior is stable over time, it's re-specified at recurring cost on every call, and a large, high-quality labeled dataset already exists in production history. The arithmetic is 900 / 1000 x $0.01 x 2,000,000 = $18,000 per month (the price is illustrative). Fine-tuning on that dataset could remove the ~900 tokens of formatting instructions and examples from every call, cutting that figure and latency while likely improving format consistency. Fine-tuned models typically cost more per token than their base models, so compare the real totals before committing. Prompt caching, where your provider offers it, can also discount a repeated prompt prefix and is worth trying first. Note what's *not* being fine-tuned: the category definitions and any policy content the classification references are knowledge that should keep coming from RAG or an explicit prompt, not get folded into the same fine-tune.

examples.title: A Decision Function Encoding the Heuristic
examples.explanation: This simplified function encodes the heuristic as a checkable priority order: freshness and citation needs are checked first and route to RAG regardless of anything else, because stable high-volume behavior or good training data doesn't change the fact that fine-tuning is unreliable for those two needs. Only then does it consider fine-tuning, and only when both a need for consistent narrow behavior *and* a large labeled dataset are present; missing either falls through to prompting, which fits the guidance that prompting is always worth trying first since it's nearly free to test. A real decision would also weigh cost, volume, and team capacity, but the ordering (knowledge needs before behavior-consistency needs, both before defaulting to prompting) captures the reasoning.

misconceptions.description: Fine-tuning is the more advanced, more powerful version of prompting or RAG, so given enough budget, it's always the strongest choice available.
misconceptions.clarification: Fine-tuning, RAG, and prompting are different levers that change different things -- weights, available context, and per-call instructions, respectively -- not a ladder of increasing power where fine-tuning sits at the top. Fine-tuning is the wrong, less reliable, and more expensive tool for knowledge and freshness problems, where RAG is cheaper and better suited whatever the budget. 'More advanced' and 'more appropriate for this problem' are different things, and treating fine-tuning as a universal upgrade leads to using it for the problems it handles worst.
misconceptions.fact: Fine-tuning, RAG, and prompting are different levers that change different things -- weights, available context, and per-call instructions, respectively -- not a ladder of increasing power where fine-tuning sits at the top.

misconceptions.description: The right way to make a model 'know' a company's product or internal documentation is to fine-tune it on that documentation.
misconceptions.clarification: This is one of the most common fine-tuning misapplications. Fine-tuning does not give a model reliable, verbatim, on-demand recall of specific facts; it adjusts weights diffusely across training, and the resulting model can paraphrase, blend, or forget specific fine-tuned facts, under the same probabilistic mechanism that produces hallucination generally. It also makes answers harder to trace to a source, and makes the knowledge stale the moment the documentation changes, requiring retraining to fix. RAG addresses the need, a model working from current, specific, sourced information, more directly, cheaply, and reliably, by retrieving the relevant text at query time instead of compressing it into weights.

exercises.prompt: Write a function choose_approach(problem: dict) -> str that returns 'rag', 'fine-tuning', or 'prompting' given a dict with boolean keys: knowledge_changes_frequently, needs_source_citation, needs_consistent_narrow_behavior_at_scale, has_large_labeled_dataset. Follow this priority: if the knowledge changes frequently OR needs source citation, choose RAG. Otherwise, if consistent narrow behavior at scale is needed AND a large labeled dataset exists, choose fine-tuning. Otherwise, default to prompting.
hints: Check the RAG conditions first, using `or` between the two knowledge and citation flags; either one alone should route to RAG.
Only after ruling out the RAG conditions should you check the fine-tuning conditions, and that check needs `and`, not `or`: both the need AND a dataset must be present.
Make sure a final fallback returns 'prompting' when neither earlier condition matched; that's the default, not an error case.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The ordering matters as much as the boolean logic. RAG is checked first, with `or`, because a freshness need or a citation need alone is reason enough to avoid fine-tuning, whatever else is true of the problem. The fine-tuning branch is second, with `and`, because fine-tuning should be chosen only when both a high-volume behavior-consistency need exists AND there's data to train on. Having just one (a behavior need with no dataset, or a dataset with no need for consistency at scale) should fall through to prompting, the safe, cheap default.

exercises.prompt: A team fine-tunes their support assistant every night on that day's current product pricing, hoping to keep it 'up to date.' This is expensive, slow to deploy (each nightly fine-tune takes hours), and the assistant is still occasionally caught quoting stale prices from earlier in the day when prices changed intraday. Identify the architectural mistake and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
# nightly_job.py (runs once per day, roughly 2am)
def nightly_retrain():
    current_pricing_data = fetch_current_pricing()
    training_examples = build_training_examples(current_pricing_data)
    fine_tune(base_model="support-assistant-v3", examples=training_examples)
    deploy_new_model_version()   # takes several hours end-to-end
hints: Pricing is described as changing 'intraday.' How does that compare to the frequency of this job, which runs once per night?
This is the same fine-tuning-for-knowledge mismatch from the explanation, applied to pricing instead of policy text. Why does fine-tuning struggle here however often you run it?
Consider what it would take to make pricing information update in near-real-time instead of on a slow, expensive nightly training cycle.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Replace nightly fine-tuning of pricing with a retrieval-backed index that
# updates the moment pricing changes, and inject the current price directly
# into the prompt at query time.

def on_pricing_change(updated_pricing_data):
    update_pricing_index(updated_pricing_data)   # near-instant, no retraining

def answer_pricing_question(question, pricing_index, generation_model):
    relevant_pricing = pricing_index.search(embed(question), top_k=3)
    context = "\n".join(p.text for p in relevant_pricing)
    prompt = (
        "Answer using ONLY the current pricing information below. "
        "If the answer isn't present, say you don't know.\n\n"
        f"Current pricing:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    )
    return generation_model.generate(prompt)
exercises.solutionExplanation: The architectural mistake is using fine-tuning, a slow, expensive batch process, to keep the assistant current on information that changes faster than the fine-tuning cycle can keep up with. Even nightly, any intraday price change is stale until the next 2am run, and the reliability problem remains whatever the frequency: fine-tuning doesn't give the model a precise lookup for a specific number, so even freshly retrained pricing is a probabilistic approximation. The fix replaces nightly retraining with a retrieval index that updates when pricing changes (a near-instant operation, nothing like a multi-hour training run) and injects the current price into the prompt when a pricing question is asked. That is both more current and more reliable, because the exact price is present as text in the context instead of approximated from training. (`embed`, `pricing_index` and the other helpers are placeholders.)

assessments.prompt: A team wants their support bot to always answer questions using the current version of their refund policy, which changes every few weeks. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Lengthen the system prompt with a general reminder to 'always be accurate about refund policy', so that the model checks its answer
Increase the model's temperature so it is more likely to guess the updated policy correctly.
Use retrieval-augmented generation over an index of the current policy document, updated whenever the policy changes.
Fine-tune the model on the refund policy text every time it changes.
assessments.explanation: This is a knowledge-freshness problem (factual content that changes regularly), which is the category RAG suits: updating a retrieval index when the policy changes is fast and cheap, and it keeps answers traceable to the current document. The “Fine-tune the model on the refund policy…” option repeats the classic fine-tuning-for-knowledge mistake: it's slow, expensive to repeat every few weeks, and doesn't reliably store an exact version of the policy text anyway. The “Increase the model's temperature…” option is unrelated: temperature governs sampling randomness, not access to correct information, and would if anything make answers less consistent. The “Lengthen the system prompt with a general…” option fails for the reason a generic 'answer accurately' instruction always fails: telling the model to be accurate about content it was never given doesn't create access to it.

assessments.prompt: A product manager asks: 'Can't we just fine-tune the model on all our documentation so it knows everything, and skip building this complicated retrieval system?' Explain, in terms a PM without a technical background could follow, why this wouldn't work as well as they expect, and what you'd propose instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fine-tuning adjusts the model through additional training so its default behavior shifts, and it's good at teaching a consistent style, tone, or answer format. But it's an unreliable way to make a model 'know' specific facts on demand, for a concrete reason: training spreads what it learns across the model's internal parameters in a diffuse, statistical way, rather than storing anything like an exact, lookup-able copy of the documents. In practice, a model fine-tuned on documentation can still get specific details wrong, blend information from different documents, or fail to reproduce a fact it saw only a few times; the tendency that makes a model occasionally state something confidently and incorrectly applies to information baked in by fine-tuning too. There are two more practical problems. Documentation changes constantly, and the fine-tuned model doesn't know about an update until another slow, costly retraining cycle, whereas updating a retrieval-based system is close to instant. And if a fine-tuned answer is wrong, there's no natural way to point at which document it came from, whereas a retrieval-based answer can show the passage it used, which matters for trust and for catching mistakes. I'd propose retrieval-augmented generation: instead of compressing the documentation into the model's training, keep it as-is and searchable, and when someone asks a question, find the relevant passages and hand them to the model with the question, so it answers from the current text rather than a fuzzy training-time memory. That is cheaper to keep up to date, easier to verify, and in practice more accurate for the 'does the model know our documentation' need the fine-tuning idea was aiming at.

assessments.prompt: According to this module, what does fine-tuning change that neither prompting nor RAG changes?
options: Fine-tuning adjusts the model's weights, persistently shifting its default behavior without needing the same instruction repeated on every call, unlike prompting (per-call instructions) or RAG (per-call retrieved context).
Fine-tuning permanently increases the size of the model's context window for all future calls.
Fine-tuning changes only the default temperature and top-p sampling values used at inference time.
Fine-tuning changes which tokenizer the model uses to encode input at inference time.
assessments.explanation: Prompting changes per-call instructions, RAG changes per-call available context, and fine-tuning is the one lever that adjusts model weights, so the shifted behavior persists without being re-specified on every call. The “Fine-tuning changes which tokenizer the model uses…”, “Fine-tuning permanently increases the size…”, and “Fine-tuning changes only the default temperature…” options each describe a change fine-tuning doesn't make; the tokenizer, the context window size, and the sampling defaults are independent of fine-tuning.

assessments.prompt: A team runs millions of calls per month and currently spends roughly 900 tokens of every single prompt re-explaining a fixed output format via instructions and few-shot examples. The desired format never changes, and the team has a large, clean, human-verified dataset of past correctly-formatted examples from production. Per this module's heuristic, what does this scenario best justify?
options: Doing nothing, since the per-call token cost of repeated instructions has no bearing on whether fine-tuning is worth pursuing.

Fine-tuning, since the behavior needing reinforcement is stable over time, is currently being re-specified at real recurring cost on every call, and a large, representative labeled dataset already exists -- exactly the scenario where fine-tuning earns its cost.
Raising the generation temperature so the model applies the format more creatively across different calls.
Switching to RAG so the formatting examples can be retrieved per call instead of being hard-coded into the prompt.
assessments.explanation: This matches the 'case where fine-tuning wins' example: a stable behavior, a recurring cost from re-specifying it every call, and a large, high-quality labeled dataset already available. The “Switching to RAG so the formatting examples…” option misapplies RAG to a behavior-consistency problem rather than a knowledge problem, the lever confusion this concept warns about. The “Raising the generation temperature so the model…” option is unrelated: temperature affects sampling randomness, not format consistency. The “Doing nothing, since the per-call token cost…” option ignores that token cost at this call volume is the recurring cost that justifies considering fine-tuning.

assessments.prompt: A team fine-tunes their support model every night on that day's product pricing, hoping to keep it current, but pricing changes intraday and the model is still occasionally caught quoting stale prices. What does this module identify as the actual underlying mistake?
options: The base model being fine-tuned is too small to memorize pricing information accurately.
The fix is to lower the fine-tuning learning rate so the model retains pricing information for longer between retraining runs.
The nightly schedule simply isn't frequent enough; running the same fine-tuning process hourly would fully solve the problem.
Fine-tuning is being used for a knowledge-freshness problem it is structurally ill-suited to regardless of how often it's run.
assessments.explanation: This is the same fine-tuning-for-knowledge mismatch as the policy-text example, applied to pricing: the unreliability of fine-tuning for exact facts, and the lag of a batch retraining cycle, don't go away by running the job more often. The “The nightly schedule simply isn't frequent enough…” option treats this as a scheduling problem, which misses that even more frequent retraining can't match near-real-time changes and still doesn't guarantee precise recall. The “The base model being fine-tuned is too…” and “The fix is to lower the fine-tuning…” options propose unrelated technical tweaks (model size, learning rate) that don't address the structural mismatch the module identifies.
